clinicalPearls: Pulmonic stenosis is overwhelmingly a congenital lesion; the valve is typically domed in isolated cases, and the pulmonic valve is only very rarely affected by the rheumatic process.
Dysplastic pulmonic valves occur as a feature of Noonan syndrome (mapped to chromosome 12), with PTPN1 gene mutations identified in roughly half of Noonan cases.
The pulmonic ejection sound (click) is the single right-sided acoustic event that DECREASES in intensity with inspiration, because elevated RV end-diastolic pressure pre-opens the valve.
As pulmonic stenosis worsens, the ejection sound migrates toward S1 and eventually becomes inaudible, the systolic murmur peaks later and may extend past A2, and P2 becomes reduced or absent.
The systolic murmur of pulmonic stenosis is mid-systolic and crescendo-decrescendo, best heard in the left second interspace, and it increases in intensity during inspiration.

The Graham Steell murmur of pulmonic regurgitation is a high-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur along the left sternal border that can be mistaken for aortic regurgitation; it tends to grow louder with inspiration.

In survivors of childhood tetralogy of Fallot or PS/pulmonary atresia repair, an RV-PA conduit lacking a valve can be freely regurgitant, producing a misleadingly low-pitched, short diastolic murmur despite significant PR and RV volume overload.

Right ventricular dysfunction from afterload mismatch appears earlier and at lower peak systolic pressures in pulmonic stenosis than left ventricular failure does in aortic stenosis, because the RV tolerates pressure overload poorly.
Cardiac output is maintained until late in pulmonic stenosis, so many patients with mild or even moderate disease are asymptomatic and are detected only by an incidental murmur or click.
A reduction in RV ejection fraction may be an early sign of hemodynamic compromise in pulmonic regurgitation, before overt symptoms develop.
Trace or mild pulmonic regurgitation of no hemodynamic significance is frequently seen on transthoracic echocardiography even when the valve is structurally normal.
Carcinoid characteristically produces mixed pulmonic valve disease, combining both regurgitation and stenosis.
harrison.pathophysiology: Pulmonic stenosis is defined hemodynamically by a systolic pressure gradient between the right ventricle and the main pulmonary artery. Sustained obstruction to RV outflow drives RV hypertrophy and prolongs systolic ejection; because the RV adapts poorly to pressure overload, dysfunction from afterload mismatch develops earlier and at lower pressures than analogous left-sided changes in aortic stenosis. The right atrial a wave rises in proportion to the higher pressures needed to fill a stiff, hypertrophied RV, and a prominent RA v wave reflects functional tricuspid regurgitation from RV and annular dilation; cardiac output is preserved until late. Pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses when mild but can worsen with age in moderate disease owing to valve thickening and calcification. In pulmonic regurgitation, severe disease causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy, creating a state of increased preload and afterload. The diastolic pressure gradient from pulmonary artery to RV that drives the regurgitant flow falls progressively through diastole, explaining the decrescendo murmur, and the murmur shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises. Forward output is preserved early but fails to augment normally with exercise and declines over time; advanced stages show marked RV and RA enlargement with elevated jugular venous pressure. PR arises from primary valve pathology, annular enlargement (e.g., long-standing severe pulmonary hypertension dilating the valve ring), or their combination, and may follow surgical relief of RV outflow obstruction or balloon valvotomy.
additionalDifferentials: Aortic regurgitation (the Graham Steell murmur of PR can mimic the AR murmur)
Other causes of a midsystolic murmur such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive physiology, or an atrial septal defect with enhanced pulmonic flow
Pulmonary hypertension as the dominant clinical problem rather than the valve lesion itself
infectionMimics: Infective endocarditis of the pulmonic valve (an etiology of both PS from bulky vegetations and PR)
nonInfectiousMimics: Carcinoid heart disease causing mixed pulmonic valve lesions
Obstructing tumors producing RV outflow obstruction that mimics valvular PS
Idiopathic dilation of the pulmonary artery / annulus causing functional PR
additionalInvestigations: ECG: right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, and right atrial enlargement in severe PS; RVH/RA enlargement may appear in PR depending on etiology and severity

Chest x-ray: poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery on the frontal view, retrosternal airspace filling from RV enlargement on the lateral view, and apex lifted off the left hemidiaphragm in some patients

Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler): definitive diagnosis in most cases, with jet velocity, gradient, RV function, pulmonary artery pressures (which should be low in PS), and associated lesions; RV systolic pressure estimated from the tricuspid regurgitant jet
Transesophageal echocardiography: better delineation of the RV outflow tract and infundibular hypertrophy when needed
Cardiac MR: greater anatomic detail and precise RV volume/function assessment, especially in repaired congenital heart disease
Cardiac catheterization: not routinely required; if performed in PS, pressures are taken just below and above the valve with attention to a possible dynamic gradient
redFlags: Exertional dyspnea or early-onset fatigue indicating severe pulmonic stenosis
Anginal chest pain from RV oxygen supply-demand mismatch, or syncope, with very severe obstruction
Destabilizing triggers (atrial fibrillation, fever, infection, anemia, pregnancy) precipitating decompensation in severe PS
Signs of right heart failure (hepatomegaly, ascites, peripheral edema) from RV systolic dysfunction
Abdominal fullness/bloating and lower-extremity swelling in progressive severe PR with RV dysfunction
harrison.prognosis: Mild pulmonic stenosis rarely progresses, whereas moderate disease may worsen with age due to valve thickening and calcification. Because cardiac output is maintained until late, many patients remain asymptomatic for years; severe disease eventually brings RV dysfunction and, uncommonly and only very late, overt right heart failure. In pulmonic regurgitation, forward output is preserved early but does not rise normally with exertion and declines over time, with a falling RV ejection fraction serving as an early marker of compromise and advanced disease producing marked RV/RA enlargement and elevated jugular venous pressure.
pitfalls: The Graham Steell murmur of PR is easily confused with aortic regurgitation along the left sternal border.
A valveless RV-PA conduit after congenital repair can give a low-pitched, short diastolic murmur that understates the true severity of PR and RV volume overload.
Doppler peak instantaneous gradient correlates only weakly with the catheterization peak-to-peak gradient; the catheter peak-to-peak value tends to track better with the Doppler MEAN gradient.
Trace or mild PR seen on echocardiography is usually of no clinical or hemodynamic consequence and should not be over-interpreted.
Relying on the systolic ejection sound can mislead in severe PS, where the click moves toward S1 and may become inaudible.
harrison.severityClassification: Pulmonic stenosis severity (normal systolic function and cardiac output): severe = peak systolic gradient >64 mmHg (mean gradient >35 mmHg, Doppler jet velocity >4 m/s); moderate = peak gradient 36-64 mmHg (jet velocity 3-4 m/s); mild = jet velocity <3 m/s (peak gradient <36 mmHg).
management: Observe mild pulmonic stenosis, which seldom progresses and requires no intervention
Relieve significant, pliable domed pulmonic stenosis with balloon valvuloplasty as first-line treatment
Refer dysplastic, calcified or heavily regurgitant valves for surgical valvotomy or pulmonary valve replacement, timed in regurgitation by right ventricular size and function
Manage right ventricular pressure or volume overload and failure with diuretic therapy
Monitor with serial echocardiography and cardiac MRI to assess the gradient, right ventricular volumes and function
Evaluate for Noonan syndrome where a dysplastic valve is present and offer genetic counselling and family screening
Manage within a cardiology or adult congenital heart disease service
